vignette:
The Weight of White Fabric

Marcus is forty-nine years old, a fashion designer of some renown whose collections have appeared in showrooms from Milan to Copenhagen. He has been married to his wife, Diane, for twenty-two years. Eighteen months ago, their nineteen-year-old daughter, Elise, was struck by a car while cycling home from university. Marcus was the first to arrive at the scene.

He remembers the white of her shirt — a blouse he had made for her himself, cut from a remnant of silk organza left over from a spring collection. He had been proud of that blouse. Now white fabric of any kind is something he cannot touch. His studio assistants have learned not to leave ivory or cream swatches on his worktable. They do not fully understand why, and Marcus has not explained.

Elise survived, but she sustained a traumatic brain injury that has left her with significant cognitive and physical impairments. She lives at home now, in a room that used to be her childhood bedroom. Marcus and Diane take turns with her care. On the surface, this looks like a family that held together. Beneath the surface, Marcus is barely holding at all.

He replays the scene constantly and involuntarily — the sound of the impact, the way her body lay at an angle that seemed geometrically wrong, the smell of petrol and cut grass. These images arrive without invitation: while he is sketching, while he is eating, in the moments just before sleep. Sleep itself has become a hostile country. He wakes between two and four in the morning most nights, heart pounding, convinced he has heard a crash somewhere in the house. He gets up and checks on Elise, then stands in the hallway for long minutes, unable to return to bed.

At work, Marcus functions — his colleagues would say he functions well — but his creative process has narrowed in ways he finds deeply troubling. He was known for his use of bold structural silhouettes and unexpected color. Now he gravitates compulsively toward dark, heavy fabrics. He cannot fully explain the impulse, only that lightness feels dishonest to him, even offensive. A junior designer recently presented a collection concept built around translucent layers and pale pastels. Marcus shut the meeting down within minutes, with a sharpness that surprised everyone in the room, including himself.

He describes feeling emotionally distant from Diane in a way that frightens him. He loves her — he is certain of that — but when she cries about Elise, which she does often and openly, he finds himself leaving the room. He tells himself he is giving her space. He knows, on some level, that he is protecting himself from something he cannot afford to feel while standing upright. Diane has started to call him absent. He does not argue with her.

What Marcus does feel, with a consistency that exhausts him, is a vigilance that never fully releases. He watches Elise eat in case she chokes. He tracks the sound of cars on their street with a precision that has become almost involuntary. When Diane is late returning home, his mind moves immediately and completely to catastrophe. He has stopped cycling — something he did for years — and finds himself unable to articulate why to anyone who asks.

He has begun to question whether the man he was before that afternoon still exists in any meaningful form. The designer who loved lightness and structure, who believed that clothing could be a form of joy — he is not sure where that person went. He comes to sessions carrying a leather notebook in which he sometimes sketches during moments of distress, filling pages with dark, angular forms that he describes as looking, to him, like something trying to hold itself together.

He does not show these sketches to anyone else. He is not sure they are about fashion at all.
